headline: History students report receiving mystical celestial weaponry instead of lunch during school recess
body:
“I was just hoping for a vegetable pulao, but the canteen lady handed me a glowing scimitar and told me to defend the borders of the classroom,” said Class 10 student Rahul Sharma, struggling to fit a five-foot broadsword into his backpack.

“The textbook said we get divine assistance to resist invaders, but so far, all I’ve received is a sudden urge to reclaim the lunch money I lost in 2022,” noted local commerce graduate Priya Menon while adjusting her newly acquired golden pauldrons.

“If these history lessons keep going at this rate, I’m going to need a much bigger parking spot for my mythical winged chariot,” remarked office commuter Sandeep Gupta as he attempted to navigate the morning traffic jam with a divine mace.

“I tried to use my assigned enchanted spear to fix the leaking tap in the staff room, but it just started reciting ancient war poetry every time I turned the knob,” explained school janitor Harish Kumar while mopping the floor with a magic shield.

“Honestly, I’d trade this legendary artifact of ultimate power for a reliable power bank, because my divine scabbard doesn't even have a USB-C port,” complained tech intern Ananya Rao after a long morning of mystical sword-wielding.
caption: Forget homework—the curriculum just got a lot heavier. Would you prefer a sword or a sandwich in your tiffin box today? #HistoryLessons #NCERT #MythicalMetals #SchoolLife (satire)
igHook: Which mystical weapon would you pick for your morning commute?
imagePrompt: A medium shot of an ordinary school backpack sitting on a wooden classroom desk, with the hilt of a metallic, ornate sword protruding from the top zipper.

sourceHeadline.title: New NCERT book says Indian kings received swords from goddesses to resist religion-driven invasions

judgeVerdict.reasoning: Candidate 7 wins by successfully blending the absurd premise with specific, grounded, and funny observational details about modern life (e.g., the scimitar not having a USB-C port, the janitor using a magic shield to mop floors). It maintains a consistently deadpan, warm tone while avoiding the repetitive 'students report receiving weapons' structure that plagues the rest of the batch.

safetyVerdict.reasoning: The article is clearly satirical, features fictional scenarios, and uses generic common names for the subjects. None of the named individuals are real public figures or private individuals involved in a way that suggests harm or defamation.
